title: After 'Ozempic Face,' Experts Now Warn of 'Ozempic Hair' Side Effect
excerpt: A major BMJ study links GLP-1 weight-loss drugs to a 37–68% higher risk of hair loss, adding to a growing list of aesthetic side effects reported by millions of users.
body:
• A University of Pennsylvania study published in The BMJ found GLP-1 users face a 37–68% higher risk of hair loss compared to patients on other diabetes drugs.
  • Experts say the hair loss, termed "Ozempic Hair," is typically temporary and driven by rapid weight loss rather than the medication itself.
  • Dermatologists estimate 25–33% of GLP-1 users experience some degree of hair shedding, with women significantly more affected than men.
  • The findings come as an estimated 15 million Americans have used GLP-1 medications in the past year.

First came "Ozempic Face" — the gaunt, hollowed-out look that became a telltale sign of rapid GLP-1-assisted weight loss. Now, dermatologists and researchers are raising alarms about another cosmetic casualty: "Ozempic Hair."

A large-scale study published in The BMJ on July 22, 2026, has provided the most rigorous evidence yet that GLP-1 receptor agonists — the drug class behind blockbuster medications like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound — carry a measurable risk of hair loss.

What the Penn Medicine Study Found

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania Health System analyzed electronic health records of tens of thousands of adults with type 2 diabetes treated between January 2019 and September 2024. They compared alopecia rates among patients starting GLP-1 receptor agonists against those beginning two other common diabetes drug classes: SGLT-2 inhibitors and DPP-4 inhibitors.

The results were striking. After adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, BMI and pre-existing conditions, GLP-1 users showed a 37% higher risk of alopecia compared with SGLT-2 inhibitor users (6.91 versus 5.04 cases per 1,000 person-years). Against DPP-4 inhibitors, the gap widened to 68% (6.53 versus 3.89 per 1,000 person-years).

The increased risk was concentrated in non-scarring alopecia — conditions where hair follicles remain intact and regrowth is possible. That form of hair loss was 53% more common among GLP-1 users than SGLT-2 users and 72% more common than DPP-4 users.

"Our findings extend previous anecdotal safety signals and provide more systematic evidence to inform clinical awareness of this potential adverse effect."

— Penn Medicine researchers, The BMJ

Why GLP-1 Drugs Trigger Hair Shedding

The culprit, experts say, is not the molecule itself but the speed of weight loss it enables. Rapid fat loss puts the body under physiological stress, triggering a condition called telogen effluvium — where hair follicles are prematurely pushed into their resting phase and begin to shed two to three months later.

Dr. Zhou at the Cleveland Clinic estimates that 25% to 33% of patients taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss experience some degree of hair thinning. Clinical trial data backs this up: 3% of adults on Wegovy reported hair loss versus 1% on placebo. For Zepbound, the numbers climbed to 4–5%, with women bearing the brunt at 7.1% compared to 0.5% of men.

Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, has confirmed to media that hair loss is an identified risk for semaglutide, adding that the risk increases once weight loss exceeds 20%.

A Booming Side-Effect Economy

The phenomenon has spawned its own retail category. Companies like MD-hair now sell £140-a-month kits of collagen gummies, scalp serums and DHT-blocking shampoos marketed specifically to "Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro users." It mirrors the trajectory of "Ozempic Face," which created demand for facial fillers and volume-restoring treatments among patients alarmed by sudden facial gauntness.

"The problem is not the drug; it is the absence of an intelligent plan that preserves muscle, protein intake and micronutrients during the weight-loss sprint."

— Dr. Anjali Mahto, dermatologist

What Patients Can Do

Dermatologists emphasize the condition is almost always temporary and manageable. Recommendations include slowing the pace of weight loss to avoid metabolic shock, maintaining high protein intake, ensuring adequate iron, zinc and vitamin B12 levels, and staying well hydrated. For active shedding, over-the-counter topical minoxidil can help stimulate regrowth.

The BMJ study's authors acknowledged limitations — they could not assess the severity or duration of hair loss, or whether it reversed after stopping medication. But they described the research as rigorous, drawing on high-quality data from a large, representative patient population.

With an estimated 15 million Americans having used GLP-1 drugs in the past year alone, the findings are likely to sharpen conversations between patients and clinicians about the full spectrum of trade-offs involved in pharmacological weight management.
